claims.text: The type of local short-range chemical ordering in CrCoNi governs strength and deformation behavior by modulating dislocation slip.
L12-type ordering creates more effective obstacles to dislocation motion than L11-type ordering.
The initial CrCoNi alloy is a near-random solid solution that may contain weak inherent short-range order.
Standard homogenization of CrCoNi predominantly produces L11-type short-range order.
Heat treatment promotes L12-type short-range order in CrCoNi.
The proposed comparison isolates L12-promoting heat treatment against a standard-homogenized, predominantly L11 control.
The nature and prevalence of L12 versus L11 short-range order act as local obstacles to dislocation motion.
L12 ordering creates more pronounced local chemical heterogeneity than L11 ordering.
The chemical heterogeneity associated with L12 order disrupts and impedes dislocation glide.
L12 ordering enhances yield strength relative to predominantly L11 ordering.
Promoting L12 order is associated with altered dislocation-slip behavior relative to the homogenized condition.
A heat-treated CrCoNi sample with dominant L12 order will have higher yield strength than the homogenized, predominantly L11 sample.
A heat-treated CrCoNi sample enriched in L12 order will exhibit different dislocation-slip behavior from the homogenized sample.
The altered slip behavior may include changed slip-plane activation and reduced slip distances.
The hypothesis is expected to apply at room temperature when composition remains uniform and secondary phases or large-scale segregation are minimized.
The mechanism may extend to other multi-component concentrated alloys processed under similar thermal conditions without secondary-phase formation.
Existing CrCoNi evidence supports a correlation between short-range-order type and mechanical behavior.
Failure to observe either a statistically significant yield-strength increase or distinct slip-behavior changes in confirmed L12-enriched samples would falsify the hypothesis.
